sections.title: Basic Concept
sections.content: In Statement and Conclusion questions, one or more statements are given along with related conclusions. You must determine whether the given conclusion definitely follows from the statement or not. The important rule is that only the information clearly given in the statement should be considered true. You should not use your general knowledge or assumptions.

sections.title: Direct Conclusion (Direct Extraction)
sections.content: Sometimes the conclusion is simply another form of the statement. The idea of the statement is expressed using slightly different words. In such cases, the conclusion is correct because it is directly based on the information given in the statement. Example: Statement: All students were present in the exam. Conclusion: No student was absent. This is a correct conclusion because both have the same meaning.

sections.title: Understanding Limits (Some vs All)
sections.content: If the statement contains the word 'some', it refers to only a few people or things, not all. Therefore, you cannot conclude 'all' from 'some'. Example: Statement: Some students are athletes. Conclusion: All students are athletes. This is incorrect because the statement only mentions 'some'.

sections.title: Public Notice Type Questions
sections.content: Sometimes the statement appears as a public notice or rule. In such questions, we need to understand the immediate purpose or effect of the notice. Example: Statement: Walking on the grass in the park is prohibited. Conclusion: People should not walk on the grass. This is a correct conclusion because that is the purpose of the notice.

sections.title: Avoid External Knowledge
sections.content: The most common mistake in Statement and Conclusion questions is that students add their general knowledge. However, in these questions only the information given in the statement is valid. If the conclusion does not directly follow from the statement, it should be considered incorrect.

sections.title: Common Exam Patterns
sections.content: 1. One statement with two conclusions. 2. Decide which conclusion definitely follows. 3. Options like 'Only I', 'Only II', 'Both', or 'None'.

sections.title: Important Rules
sections.content: 1. The conclusion must follow only from the statement. 2. If the statement says 'some', you cannot conclude 'all'. 3. If the statement clearly expresses something, the opposite conclusion will be incorrect. 4. Do not use assumptions or imagination.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Using general knowledge. 2. Not understanding the difference between 'some' and 'all'. 3. Not reading the statement carefully. 4. Ignoring new words hidden in the conclusion.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In Statement and Conclusion questions, always read the statement carefully and check whether the conclusion definitely follows from it. If the conclusion introduces new information or assumptions, it will be incorrect.

tricks.title: Think Only From the Statement
tricks.explanation: While deriving the conclusion, use only the information given in the statement. Do not include outside knowledge.
tricks.example: Statement: All books are useful. Conclusion: Some books are useful. This is correct because 'all' includes 'some'.

tricks.title: Do Not Assume All from Some
tricks.explanation: If the statement contains the word 'some', you cannot conclude 'all'.
tricks.example: Statement: Some players run fast. Conclusion: All players run fast. This is incorrect.

tricks.title: Identify Direct Meaning
tricks.explanation: If the conclusion repeats the statement in different words, it may be correct.
tricks.example: Statement: All cars are vehicles. Conclusion: No car is separate from vehicles.

tricks.title: Be Careful with New Words
tricks.explanation: If the conclusion contains a word that is not mentioned in the statement, it is often incorrect.
tricks.example: Statement: Some teachers are strict. Conclusion: Some teachers teach mathematics. This is incorrect because mathematics is not mentioned.

tricks.title: Understand Public Notices
tricks.explanation: If the statement is a notice or rule, derive the conclusion based on its purpose.
tricks.example: Statement: Smoking is prohibited here. Conclusion: People should not smoke here.

tricks.title: All Implies Some
tricks.explanation: If the statement contains 'all', the conclusion with 'some' is always correct.
tricks.example: Statement: All doctors are educated. Conclusion: Some doctors are educated.

tricks.title: Avoid Reverse Conclusions
tricks.explanation: Students sometimes reverse the meaning of the statement, which leads to an incorrect conclusion.
tricks.example: Statement: All cats are animals. Conclusion: All animals are cats. This is incorrect.

tricks.title: Check for Certainty
tricks.explanation: A conclusion is correct only if it definitely follows from the statement.
tricks.example: Statement: Some children draw pictures. Conclusion: Some children are artists. This is not certain.

tricks.title: Compare Two Conclusions Separately
tricks.explanation: If two conclusions are given, examine each one independently.
tricks.example: Statement: All fruits are sweet. Conclusion I: Some fruits are sweet. Conclusion II: Some sweet things are fruits.

tricks.title: Read Carefully
tricks.explanation: Small words like some, all, or none can completely change the meaning of the question. So read the statement carefully.
tricks.example: Statement: No student came late. Conclusion: All students came on time.
